content: Preventive chemotherapy, also known as deworming, is strongly recommended for young children aged 12–23 months, preschool children aged 24–59 months, and school-aged children (5–12 years) living in areas where the prevalence of soil-transmitted helminth infections is 20% or higher. This intervention aims to reduce the burden of worm infections. In areas where the prevalence exceeds 50%, biannual administration of deworming medications is advised. For children under 24 months, a reduced dose of 200 mg is recommended. Preventive chemotherapy using single-dose albendazole (400 mg) or mebendazole (500 mg) is also recommended for non-pregnant adolescent girls (10–19 years) and non-pregnant women of reproductive age (15–49 years) in areas with a soil-transmitted helminth prevalence of 20% or higher. This intervention helps reduce the worm burden in these populations. In areas with a prevalence exceeding 50%, biannual administration is recommended. For pregnant women living in areas where the prevalence of hookworm or Trichuris trichiura infections is 20% or higher and where anemia is a severe public health problem (prevalence of 40% or higher), preventive chemotherapy is conditionally recommended after the first trimester. This aims to reduce the burden of hookworm and T. trichiura infections. The most recent estimates of anemia prevalence can be accessed through the WHO-hosted Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System (VMNIS). The current guidelines update and replace previous recommendations from the WHO publication on preventive chemotherapy for human helminthiasis. These guidelines also complement operational guidance for helminth control in school-aged children. School-aged children are defined as those between 5 and 12 years of age, although in some settings, the upper age range may extend to 14 years. These ages correspond to compulsory school years in most regions, providing an opportunity to address the nutritional needs of this group. Soil-transmitted helminth infections, caused by Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), and hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus), are among the most common infections in humans. These infections are most prevalent in areas with inadequate sanitation and warm, tropical climates. Transmission occurs through ingestion of eggs or larvae in contaminated soil or, in the case of hookworms, through skin penetration by larvae. Reinfection is common in contaminated environments, as these worms do not multiply within the human host. Globally, nearly 2 billion people are infected with soil-transmitted helminths, including approximately 270 million preschool children and over 550 million school-aged children. Around 250 million girls and women live in endemic areas. The highest burden is observed in sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas, and Asia. These infections are grouped together for control purposes due to their similar geographic distribution, treatment methods, diagnostic tools, and health impacts. The morbidity caused by soil-transmitted helminth infections is well-documented. Hookworm infections, for example, lead to blood loss and anemia due to the parasite feeding on blood and causing mechanical damage to the intestinal mucosa. Heavy infections can result in daily iron loss exceeding the nutritional requirements of a healthy school-aged child. Hookworm infections are among the leading causes of anemia globally. Similarly, Ascaris lumbricoides infections can cause significant morbidity, including malnutrition and intestinal obstruction. Preventive chemotherapy is an effective public health intervention to reduce the burden of soil-transmitted helminth infections. Albendazole and mebendazole are well-tolerated medications with minor and transient side effects. However, preventive chemotherapy alone does not break the cycle of infection and reinfection. Therefore, populations in contaminated environments require frequent administration of deworming medications. Integrated programs that include water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions are essential to sustainably control soil-transmitted helminth infections. Deworming programs should be accompanied by health and hygiene promotion to reduce transmission through behaviors such as handwashing, wearing footwear, and proper disposal of feces. Routine monitoring and evaluation of these programs are necessary to assess their effectiveness and inform decisions on continuation or cessation. Research gaps remain in areas such as diagnostic indicators for identifying at-risk populations, alternative anthelmintic medications in case of drug resistance, and the impact of co-interventions on nutritional outcomes and reinfection rates. Further studies are needed to document adverse effects in specific populations, such as individuals living with HIV, breastfeeding mothers, and pregnant women. The WHO will continue to monitor research developments in preventive chemotherapy and update these guidelines as new evidence becomes available. These recommendations aim to guide policymakers, health professionals, and program managers in designing and implementing effective interventions to control soil-transmitted helminth infections and improve public health outcomes.
